11.quote_or_event: “O rainbird, the One unto whom you call - everyone longs for that Lord. When He grants His Grace, it rains, and the forests and fields blossom forth in their greenery... O Nanak! The Ambrosial Nectar rains down forever; the Lord gives it to the Gurmukh.”
11.explanation: In the monsoon raag Malar, Guru Amar Das moves from real rain, which turns forests and fields green, to amrit (ambrosial nectar) raining down without end. Rain and amrit are spoken of in the same breath.
11.tie_back: Like the Kural, Gurbani connects life-giving rain with amrit, the deathless nectar.
11.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1281, Raag Malar, Vaar Malar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
11._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted lines); the rain-amrit pairing is genuine, but in Gurbani the nectar is ultimately the Name, a spiritual meaning beyond the Kural's literal praise of rain.

12.quote_or_event: “He commands the god of rain, and the rain pours down in torrents. Corn and wealth are produced in great abundance and prosperity... He reaches out and gives sustenance to all beings. Eating this, peace is produced.”
12.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes a single chain: rain falls, grain grows, and people eat and are at peace. The rain itself comes from God's command.
12.tie_back: The Kural's point is that rain makes the food and nourishes those who eat it. This salok traces the same path from rain to food to the eater's contentment.
12.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1281, Raag Malar, Vaar Malar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
12._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks one omitted line); a strong match on rain as the source of food, but it lacks the Kural's second claim that rain is itself the drink.

13.quote_or_event: “The hunger of the hungry is not appeased, even by piling up loads of worldly goods.”
13.explanation: In the opening stanza of Japji, Guru Nanak says that heaping up material goods never satisfies hunger. The deeper hunger is only met by obeying God's hukam (will).
13.tie_back: The Kural pictures a world ringed by oceans that still starves without rain. Japji likewise says that surrounding yourself with plenty does not end hunger.
13.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
13._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, but next-best only: Japji speaks of spiritual craving, whereas the Kural is about literal famine from failed rain.

14.quote_or_event: “Make your mind the farmer, good deeds the farm, modesty the water, and your body the field. Let the Lord’s Name be the seed, contentment the plow, and your humble dress the fence.”
14.explanation: Guru Nanak, who spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, uses the farmer's whole round of work as a picture of the spiritual life. Water is one of its essential inputs.
14.tie_back: The Kural pictures the ploughman as the most hard-working of people, whose labour stops without rain. Guru Nanak builds a spiritual farm in which water is a necessary part.
14.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
14._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the farmer, plough and water imagery and Sikh respect for agricultural labour (kirat karni), but it is a metaphor and does not make the Kural's point that ploughing stops in drought.

15.quote_or_event: “Some sing that He fashions the body, and then again reduces it to dust. Some sing that He takes life away, and then again restores it.”
15.explanation: Japji lists the ways people praise God: as the one who both destroys and restores, who takes life away and gives it back.
15.tie_back: The Kural gives rain this double power to ruin and to raise up again. Sikh scripture gives the same double power to God working through hukam.
15.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 3, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
15._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the destroy-and-restore structure is exact, but Gurbani gives it to God rather than to rain, as the Kural pointedly does.

16.quote_or_event: “First, there is life in the water, by which everything else is made green.”
16.explanation: Arguing against ideas of ritual impurity, Guru Nanak notes that life begins in water and that water is what turns everything green.
16.tie_back: This is the Kural's point in one line: without water from the sky, not even a blade of grass turns green.
16.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
16._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match on water as the precondition of all green life, though the surrounding salok is about impurity rather than rainfall.

17.quote_or_event: “Whatever he takes, he does not give back. Seeking to earn more and more, he is troubled and uneasy.”
17.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the man who prospers by taking without ever giving back. Sikh ethics answers this with vand chhakna, sharing what one has earned.
17.tie_back: The Kural's cloud diminishes the sea if it takes water and never returns it. Commentators read that as a warning about people who take from their community without giving back, which is exactly the person this salok condemns.
17.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
17._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it matches only the Kural's traditional social reading (taking without returning), not its literal water-cycle image.

18.quote_or_event: At Hardwar, while pilgrims threw water east as offerings to their ancestors, Guru Nanak threw water west. He said he was watering his fields in Punjab, and asked how their water could reach ancestors so much farther away. He then taught that the true sacrifice of the age was giving food to those who remember God's Name.
18.explanation: In Macauliffe's account of Guru Nanak's life, the Guru turns a water-offering ritual into a lesson. Water is for living fields, and real worship is feeding people and remembering the Name, not offerings to gods or the dead.
18.tie_back: The Kural says worship of the celestials stops when rain fails. Sikhism agrees that water sustains life but rejects such ritual worship and puts feeding the hungry in its place.
18.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 50-52
18._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the Hardwar episode (verified in Macauliffe, drawn from the Janamsakhi tradition and hagiographic in detail) links water and worship, but Sikh teaching rejects the very ritual worship whose survival the Kural defends.

19.quote_or_event: “Pilgrimages, austere discipline, compassion and charity - these, by themselves, bring only an iota of merit.”
19.explanation: Japji names the same pair the Kural does, austerity (tap) and charity (daan), and says that alone they earn only a speck of merit. What matters is cleansing oneself with the Name.
19.tie_back: The Kural says both charity and austerity collapse without rain. Japji puts them in a different order: both are real goods, but both depend on something deeper, the Name.
19.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
19._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it names the same two virtues and makes them conditional on something more basic, but that foundation is the Name, not rain, and Sikhism downplays austerity, which the Kural values.

20.quote_or_event: “Food and wealth are produced in abundance when it rains, if it is the Will of God. Consuming it, the minds of His creatures are satisfied, and they adopt the lifestyle of the way.”
20.explanation: Guru Amar Das links rain to food, food to a contented mind, and a contented mind to living rightly, the way of life.
20.tie_back: This is the Kural's own conclusion: right conduct, like the world itself, cannot carry on without rain.
20.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1282, Raag Malar, Vaar Malar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
20._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a strikingly close match tracing rain to food to right living, though Gurbani places the whole sequence under God's will.
